name: VL6180X time-of-flight rangefinder breakout
//: A carrier for ST's VL6180X. WHICH carrier matters more than usual and most of the unknowns below are about that, not about the chip.

needs.note: Only needed if the sensor is to wake the host from sleep. It ranges continuously by itself and asserts this pin on a threshold, which is the only way a sleeping host can be told about a hand.

power.note: the carrier regulates down to the die's 2.8 V

die_supply_v.why_it_matters: The DIE is a 2.8 V part. A bus pulled to 3.3 V meets a pad powered from 2.8 V, and whether that is safe depends entirely on whether the carrier level-shifts.
die_supply_v.note: A 2.8 V LDO on the carrier feeds it from VIN, so the die never sees the host's 3.3 V.

carrier_has_level_shifters.source: Pololu's own schematic for carrier #2489, PCB revision irs09a: https://www.pololu.com/file/0J960/vl6180x-time-of-flight-distance-sensor-carrier-schematic.pdf (document pololu-2489-schematic)
carrier_has_level_shifters.note: Q1A and Q1B, the usual two-MOSFET bidirectional shifter, with 10k to VIN on the host side and 10k to the 2.8 V VDD on the die side. So SDA and SCL are safe to drive at 3.3 V, and the bus already has 10k pull-ups without the host adding any.

carrier_pulls_up_the_interrupt.source: Pololu's own schematic for carrier #2489, PCB revision irs09a: https://www.pololu.com/file/0J960/vl6180x-time-of-flight-distance-sensor-carrier-schematic.pdf (document pololu-2489-schematic)
carrier_pulls_up_the_interrupt.note: R6, 47k to VDD — which is 2.8 V, not the host's 3.3 V — with R8 1k in series out to the header. So the interrupt idles near 2.8 V. That clears an ESP32-S3's input high threshold, but a host adding its own pull-up to 3.3 V is fighting a divider rather than helping, and the level it settles at is what an ext1 wake reads.

idle_current_ma.why_it_matters: It free-runs while the host sleeps, so on a battery design it is one of the two or three loads that decide the answer.

module_has_i2c_pullups.source: Pololu's own schematic for carrier #2489, PCB revision irs09a: https://www.pololu.com/file/0J960/vl6180x-time-of-flight-distance-sensor-carrier-schematic.pdf (document pololu-2489-schematic)
module_has_i2c_pullups.note: 10 k to VIN on the host side of the Q1A/Q1B shifter, on SDA and SCL (the carrier_has_level_shifters fact). Corrected 2026-10-03 (P81): the host_parts reasons used to say the module carries none.

i2c_pullup_ohms.source: Pololu's own schematic for carrier #2489, PCB revision irs09a: https://www.pololu.com/file/0J960/vl6180x-time-of-flight-distance-sensor-carrier-schematic.pdf (document pololu-2489-schematic)
i2c_pullup_ohms.note: to VIN, the host's supply, on the host side of the level shifter

host_requirements: I2C needs pull-ups. The host's own internal pull-ups are tens of kiloohms and far too weak; size them against the bus speed and the cable, not by habit.
If this sits on a ribbon away from the board, the ribbon's capacitance is part of the bus and belongs in the rise-time budget.

Behind a window, range-ignore must be calibrated or the window's own reflection reads as a target — and on an interrupt-driven design that is a wake loop, which is worse for the battery than never sleeping.
//footprint: SEVEN pads, not five. It said pinrow5 until 2026-09-25 — the count of pins this design WIRES, not the count of pads Pololu put on the carrier. The file's own //pin_order note said seven all along. Consequence: emit_board labelled a pad that does not exist, that port got no position, and tscircuit's autorouter died reading its x, which does not fail loudly — it leaves the whole board with zero traces.
//on_board: It has to look out through the enclosure, so it is never on the PCB. The board carries the mating header; body_mm is the carrier's own outline, so a generated layout keeps room for it should it plug straight in.

body_mm.source: Pololu's dimension drawing for #2489, PCB irs09a, dated 9 August 2016 — view 1, Board dimensions (top view): 12.7 mm [500 mil] wide, 17.8 mm [700 mil] tall; board edge tolerance ±0.3 mm
body_mm.note: As the drawing stands: the 7-pin header runs down the 17.8 mm edge at 2.54 mm, its first hole 1.27 mm from the edge (view 2). The board is 1.02 mm thick with 1.2 mm of parts above it (view 4, Profile); two 2.2 mm mounting holes.

//variant: WHICH BREAKOUT THIS DESCRIBES, because they are not interchangeable. Four exist and they differ in size, pin count, pin order and what is on the board: Pololu #2489 has 7 pins, the current Adafruit 3316 has 6 and no 2v8 pin, the older Adafruit had 7 in another order, and the generic boards vary between factories. The facts below are read off Pololu's schematic and hold for that carrier ONLY. On another board they are not approximately right, they are unknown.

pin_order_proof.source: Pololu's 7-pin header reads VDD · VIN · GND · SDA · SCL · GPIO0/CE · GPIO1. This file wires five of them; pad 1 (VDD, the 2.8 V rail brought out for reference) and pad 6 (GPIO0/CE, the chip-enable) are real pads this design does not use, so they stay empty. Read off Pololu's own schematic for carrier #2489.

wokwi.note: answers I2C at 0x29 with a range the `distance` control sets; always reports a good status and a ready sample

host_parts.why: the carrier's own 10 k to VIN are weak for anything but a short bus; 4.7 k in parallel makes about 3.2 k, which suits 100-400 kHz — a ribbon wants less (the bin chose 2.2 k for its cable)
the same, for the clock line
